questions.question: Ilanga Ltd has sales of R3 600 000, cost of sales R2 250 000, other operating income R90 000, operating expenses R840 000, interest income R15 000, interest expense R75 000 and a tax rate of 27 percent. Build the statement of comprehensive income to net profit after tax, naming each profit level.
questions.expected_answer: Sales R3 600 000 less cost of sales R2 250 000 gives gross profit of R1 350 000 — a mark-up of 60 percent on cost. Add other operating income of R90 000 for gross operating income of R1 440 000, deduct operating expenses of R840 000 for operating profit of R600 000. Add interest income of R15 000 to reach R615 000, deduct interest expense of R75 000 for net profit before tax of R540 000. Income tax at 27 percent is R145 800, leaving net profit after tax of R394 200. The three named levels — gross profit, operating profit and net profit — measure buying and pricing, running the operation, and financing respectively. Dividends never appear among the expenses: they are a distribution of profit shown in the retained income note.

questions.question: Complete Ilanga's cash flow statement: net profit before tax R540 000, depreciation R180 000, interest expense R75 000; inventories up R40 000, receivables up R25 000, payables up R32 000; interest paid R75 000, tax paid R140 000, dividends paid R250 000; fixed assets bought R450 000, fixed deposit increased R20 000; shares issued R200 000, loan repaid R60 000; opening cash R163 000. Show that it closes on the balance sheet's cash figure.
questions.expected_answer: Operating: start with net profit before tax R540 000, add back depreciation R180 000 and interest expense R75 000 for R795 000. Working capital: inventories up R40 000 is cash out, receivables up R25 000 is cash out, payables up R32 000 is cash in — cash generated from operations R762 000. Deduct interest paid R75 000, tax paid R140 000 and dividends paid R250 000 — net cash from operating activities R297 000. Investing: fixed assets R450 000 out plus fixed deposit R20 000 out — R470 000 used. Financing: shares issued R200 000 in less loan repaid R60 000 — R140 000 in. Net change: 297 000 minus 470 000 plus 140 000 is a decrease of R33 000. Opening cash R163 000 gives closing cash R130 000, exactly the cash and cash equivalents figure in current assets — the statement closes the loop, which is the proof it is right.

questions.question: Name and explain the three types of audit opinion, state to whom the audit report is addressed and why, and explain why auditor independence matters to users of the statements.
questions.expected_answer: An unqualified opinion states that the financial statements fairly present the company's position — a clean opinion with no reservations. A qualified opinion states they are fairly presented except for specific matters the auditor lists — reliable, but read the exceptions. A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor could not obtain enough evidence to express any opinion, and an adverse opinion means the statements do not fairly present the position — both are serious alarms. The report is addressed to the shareholders, because the directors prepare statements about their own stewardship and the auditor is the owners' independent check on the managers — never the reverse. Independence matters because the entire value of the report is the credibility of the signature: an auditor with shares in the client, close personal ties to directors, or fee dependence on one client has a motive to soften the verdict, and a softened verdict misleads every user downstream — banks assessing loans, investors buying shares, SARS assessing tax — who all rely on that opinion. An audit gives reasonable assurance based on targeted sampling, not a guarantee, which is why the company's own internal controls remain essential.
